Q1.answer: Only inferable late: whether forecasting error under a post-training level shift comes from stale normalization statistics (versus model capacity), and whether per-window (rolling) normalization reduces it. The Abstract and Introduction never state a problem or question; the Discussion admits the question was 'not stated'.
Q1.missing: An explicit problem/question statement in the Abstract or Introduction.

Q2.answer: Deployed series (e.g. energy load) can change level after training, and standard normalization uses training statistics, which may then be stale. Every supporting statement is an unfilled citation placeholder, so importance is asserted, not established.
Q2.missing: Evidence or citations for prevalence and cost of level shifts; all four claims are [CITATION NEEDED].

Q3.missing: The paper notes that many normalization variants exist but never says what they lack or how RWN relates to existing per-window/instance normalization methods.

Q4.answer: Generated a synthetic hourly load series (SynthLoad, daily+weekly cycles, Gaussian noise), injected level shifts of 0.2-0.8 training SDs, and compared an MLP (64 hidden units, same budget, 5 seeds) under three normalizations: training statistics (baseline), rolling-window normalization over the last 48 steps (RWN), and RWN-fixed (statistics frozen after the first 48 post-shift steps). Reported MAE.
Q4.missing: Series length, train/test split, input and horizon lengths, when the shift occurs, whether outputs are de-normalized, and the units of MAE.

Q5.missing: No rationale for RWN, the 48-step window, the MLP, or synthetic data; the only implicit reason is that rolling statistics would track a level shift.

Q6.answer: No-shift comparison of baseline vs RWN; shifted comparisons at s = 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8 (baseline vs RWN); an ablation freezing the statistics (RWN-fixed), reported only at s = 0.6. 5 seeds each.

Q7.answer: RWN reduced MAE by 11-29% across s = 0.2-0.6 relative to the baseline, with seed spread said to be small; no-shift MAE was 0.409 +/- 0.007 (RWN) vs 0.412 +/- 0.006 (baseline).
Q7.missing: Per-shift MAE values and seed SDs for s = 0.2-0.6; Figure 1 itself is absent.

Q8.answer: On this one synthetic series, with one MLP and one 48-step window, rolling normalization lowers MAE under moderate level shifts (0.2-0.6 SD) and costs no detectable accuracy without shift; freezing the statistics after adaptation keeps part (reportedly about two thirds) of the gain at s = 0.6.

Q9.answer: No benefit at s = 0.8 (overlapping seed spreads). Nothing about real data, other shift types (trend, variance, seasonal changes), other window sizes, or other models. It does not establish that capacity is not responsible, because capacity was never varied. The two-thirds figure cannot be checked from reported numbers.

Q10.answer: Per the Discussion: evidence that shift-induced error in this setting stems from stale normalization statistics rather than capacity, and that per-window normalization removes most of it for moderate shifts with no unshifted cost, with about a third of the gain depending on continued adaptation. The Abstract and Conclusion describe no contribution beyond 'several experiments'.

Q11.answer: Synthetic data only; untuned window (48); only level shifts; capacity held constant not varied; single model; 5 seeds; ablation at one shift magnitude.

Q12.answer: Normalizing each input window with its recent statistics cut MAE by roughly 11-29% under moderate level shifts on synthetic load data with no no-shift cost, did not help at the largest shift, and lost part of its gain if adaptation stopped.

objective_discrepancies: The objective frames a clear three-part question (shift robustness, no-shift cost, dependence on adaptation); the paper never states it up front and the Discussion admits the question was not stated.
The objective asks readers to know what was found and where it stops; the Abstract and Conclusion report no findings or boundaries at all.
The paper reframes the contribution as normalization-vs-capacity attribution, which is not in the objective and is not supported by the design.
The adaptation-dependence part of the objective is supported only at s = 0.6, and the numbers needed to check it are missing.
